t71b_secsc:
## Close the Session and Return to Life

When you're done, end it for real. Otherwise processing can go on and on, until it's just another way to not live your life. Take a look around and name where you are (yes, out loud, even if it feels silly). Then feel something solid, your feet on the floor or the chair under you, and unclench your jaw and your hands, which have probably been at it this whole time.

Then pick the next normal thing you'll do, like making food or going to sleep, and tell your little one, "That's enough for today. We're going back to the life we're building." Nothing has to be resolved first, and whatever you're still feeling can come along. Going back to your life is part of the healing, too.
t71b_secjl:
## Just Like Me

This one works best on a steadier day, when thinking about other people won't pull you out of your own shoes. Name the feeling plainly. Lonely, say. Then think of how many people are feeling that exact thing right now, and wanting it to stop, just like you. Some of them make it worse trying to get away from it. Just like you, sometimes. 😅 Wish all of you, you first, enough support to stay with it, so the pain stops with you.

You don't need any special breathing. And forgiving whoever hurt you, or imagining their childhood? Also not required, and neither is getting in touch with them (if that ever happens, it's its own decision, made on a calmer day than this). The point is just to stop treating a feeling this many people have had as proof that you, specifically, are defective.
t71b_x3a: Watch the narrator's tone. A grandpa on the porch can be warm about the hard parts too. If yours starts sneering instead, that's the prosecutor sneaking back into the room, so stop there. Same goes if the shame gets worse, or everything starts to feel kind of unreal, because more distance won't fix that. On a good day, though, it's a sweet moment to ask the younger you in that story what they need from you now.
t71b_x3b: And who's telling it, a kind grandpa or someone smirking? If it's the smirk, stop, because that means the trial's back on. Stop too if the shame gets louder, or you start feeling spacey and unreal, since more distance won't fix that. But if it lands, there's a younger you sitting right there in the story, so ask them what they need from you now, and maybe give them a little of it.
t71b_x3c: Do keep an ear on who's narrating, though. If the voice starts sneering, like it's making fun of the younger you, stop right there (that's the courtroom creeping back in). Same if you feel more ashamed, or kind of floaty and unreal, since more distance won't help with that. And when it goes well, it's a good time to check in with the younger you in that story. What do they need from you now?
t71b_jwc: Sometimes your little one just won't talk, and picturing them gets you nowhere either. That's when it's worth grabbing a pen and switching hands. Your clumsy hand already writes like a first grader, so make it your little one's, and have it put down whatever scared or hurt stuff is really there (no making it up to fill the silence). Your usual hand answers as the grown-up who's got their back. And if the protective part grabs the pen first? Then let it use the clumsy hand first. The guard gets to talk before your little one does.
t71b_jwe: If your little one goes quiet on you, try writing it out with your other hand. It's clumsy, and the letters come out looking like a first grader wrote them, which is perfect, since that's whose hand it is now. Let it put down whatever scared or hurt feelings are really there, nothing made up. Your usual hand answers as the grown-up who's got their back. Does the protective part grab the pen first? Then it gets the clumsy hand first, like a bouncer who has to check you out before anyone gets in.
t71b_oic: This one's about as low-tech as it gets. You wake up and pick one small thing to watch for, like "Today I'll notice one hook before I act on it." Honestly, one is plenty, since hooks are sneaky and don't announce themselves. Then at night, before bed, you look back over the day the way a friend would, no cross-examination. Where did you catch it? Where did it run the whole routine anyway? What's one small repair, or some little thing that would protect your little one tomorrow?
t71b_oih: Pick one small intention when you wake up, like "Today I'll notice one hook before I act on it." Then see what the day does with it. At night, before you sleep, go back over it gently, the way a friend would. Maybe you caught the hook at lunch. Maybe it ran its whole routine anyway (hooks are sneaky like that). So what's the next small repair, or some little thing that would protect your little one?
